title: The Slave No One Could Own
author: Epictetus
wiifm: Epictetus was born a slave, walked with a limp, was thrown out of Rome by an emperor, and never wrote a word. Yet his lectures, taken down by a student, reached Marcus Aurelius and, nearly two thousand years later, an American pilot in a North Vietnamese prison. We follow the boy whose name meant acquired from a Roman household to a schoolroom on the Greek coast. You will come away with the sharpest tool in Stoicism, the split between what is up to you and what is not, and the habit of refusing to sign a first impression.

b: He was born around 50 AD in Hierapolis, a spa town in Phrygia, in what is now south-western Turkey, famous for its white terraces of hot springs. We do not know his real name, or whether his mother ever had the chance to give him one. The name history kept, Epiktetos, is Greek for acquired. It is not really a name. It is a label for property.

At some point as a child he was taken to Rome as a slave. Of his family, his early years and how he got there, we know nothing at all. What we do know is that for the rest of his life he thought harder than anyone in the ancient world about one question: what, if anything, belongs to a person whose body belongs to someone else?

He walked with a limp. The ancient sources disagree about why. One tradition says he had been lame from childhood, perhaps from rheumatism. Another tells a crueller story, which we will come to. The honest position is that we do not know.

Keep this beginning in mind for everything that follows. When Epictetus says your body, your reputation and your property are not truly yours, he is not playing with a clever paradox. He is describing his own legal condition, and then asking what was left.
ch.cap: A slave boy is led away from Hierapolis's white terraces

b: His owner in Rome was Epaphroditus, a former slave himself who had risen to be one of Nero's secretaries, a powerful figure at court. Epaphroditus was with Nero at the very end in 68, when the cornered emperor was helped to stab himself. Years later the Emperor Domitian had Epaphroditus executed, reportedly for giving exactly that help. Epictetus grew up in the household of a man who lived at the dangerous centre of power.

Here is the story the sources disagree about. The pagan writer Celsus told it in the second century, and we have it only because the Christian writer Origen quoted it in order to argue with it. Epictetus's master was twisting his leg. Epictetus said calmly, you will break it. The master kept twisting, and the leg broke. Epictetus said: did I not tell you that you would break it?

It is almost certainly too good to be true. It reaches us third-hand, through two writers with their own purposes, and it contradicts the tradition that he was lame from childhood. But it survived for a reason. It is a perfect picture of the doctrine. The master had complete power over the leg and none at all over the sentence.

Epaphroditus did one thing that changed the history of philosophy. He let his slave attend the lectures of Musonius Rufus, the most serious Stoic teacher in Rome, a man who argued that women should study philosophy just as men did. It was not necessarily kindness, since an educated slave was a status symbol in a wealthy house. But it gave Epictetus his life's work. At some point, by some means nobody recorded, he was freed, and he began to teach.
ch.cap: Calm Epictetus warns his master: you will break it

b: Philosophers made Roman emperors nervous. They talked about tyranny, praised dead opponents of the regime, and could not be bribed with things they claimed not to want. Around 93 AD, though some date it a few years earlier, the Emperor Domitian expelled the philosophers from Rome and Italy. Epictetus, by now a teacher with a following, had to go.

He crossed to Nicopolis, a city on the western coast of Greece founded by Augustus to celebrate his victory at Actium. There he opened a school, and there he stayed for the rest of his long life. Young men from good Roman families came to him, many of them on their way to careers in government. One late source claims the Emperor Hadrian counted him among his friends.

He lived on almost nothing. For most of his life he had no wife and no household, until, a later writer tells us, he took in a child a friend was about to abandon and found a woman to help him raise it. He was poor by circumstance and by choice, and that matters. When he tells you not to need things, he is not speaking from a villa.

Around 108, one of those well-born students, a young Greek called Flavius Arrianus, began writing down what his teacher said in class. Arrian would later become a Roman consul, governor of Cappadocia and the best surviving historian of Alexander the Great. But his first book was a transcript of an old lame teacher, and it is the only reason we know what Epictetus thought.
ch.cap: Expelled from Rome, Epictetus sails for Nicopolis

ch.h: A handbook and a lost life
b: Epictetus wrote nothing himself. Arrian recorded his lectures and conversations in eight books of Discourses, of which four survive. He then boiled the most useful material down into a short digest called the Enchiridion, which means the handbook, or more literally the thing you hold in your hand. It runs to about forty pages. Arrian also wrote a life of his teacher, which is lost.

In a covering letter Arrian says he tried to keep his teacher's actual words, and it shows. The Discourses read like transcripts because they more or less are. Students interrupt. Epictetus mocks them, loses patience, tells stories, and takes his images from the gymnasium and the farmyard rather than the lecture hall. It is the least decorated prose in ancient philosophy: a man talking, in a room, to young people he expects to go out and do something.

And then comes the chain that links the week. These notes were copied and passed from hand to hand for decades, until the Stoic senator Junius Rusticus lent his own copy to the young heir to the throne, Marcus Aurelius. A former slave's ideas reached the most powerful man of the age through a student's notebook. Marcus quotes or echoes him throughout the Meditations.
So what was in the notebook that mattered so much? It begins with a single division.
ch.cap: Young Arrian writes down his old teacher's words

b: The handbook opens with the division everything else rests on. Some things are up to us and some are not. Up to us are our judgements, our impulses, our desires and our aversions: in a word, whatever is our own doing. Not up to us are our body, our property, our reputation and our position: in a word, whatever is not our own doing.

Modern retellings soften this into focus on what you can control, which is a productivity slogan and loses the sting. Epictetus is saying something much more aggressive. Your reputation is not yours. Your health is not yours. Your business is not yours. Even your children are not yours. They are all on loan, run by forces indifferent to you. The one thing you truly own is the faculty that judges and chooses, which he calls prohairesis, the reasoned will. No tyrant, illness, bankruptcy or bereavement can reach it without your cooperation.

If you treat only what is yours as yours, he promises, nobody will ever compel you or hinder you, and you will blame and accuse no one. This is a kind of freedom that was literally available to a slave. Epaphroditus owned Epictetus's body and could do what he liked with it. He could not make Epictetus agree to a false judgement. For Epictetus that was not a metaphor. It was a precise statement about where coercion stops.

For anyone running a business, the practical version is a two-column audit. On the left, what is truly up to you: your pricing discipline, the quality of your hiring, whether you read the contract, your cash buffer, your conduct in a hard meeting. On the right, what is not: interest rates, a competitor's funding, a client's internal politics, an algorithm change, what people say about you. Then look at where last month's worry actually went. Most people find it nearly all on the right, with a fixable problem sitting untouched on the left.
ch.cap: Epictetus divides the world: up to us, and not

ch.h: Wait for me a little, impression
b: From that division comes the most quoted line in Stoicism. People are disturbed not by things, but by their judgements about things. Death is nothing terrible, Epictetus says, or it would have seemed so to Socrates. The terror lies in the judgement that death is terrible.

The mechanism is worth spelling out, because the slogan on its own is useless. An impression arrives, and it arrives already dressed. Not some numbers on a screen, but we are going under. Epictetus taught three disciplines, of desire, of action and of assent, and the third is about the tiny gap between an impression arriving and your agreeing to it. You cannot stop impressions coming. You can decline to sign them.

His instruction is to talk back. Wait for me a little, impression, he tells his students to say. Let me see what you are and what you represent. Let me test you. The gap is small at first and it widens with practice. Ask an untrained person what upset them this week and they will describe events. Ask a trained one and they will describe judgements they agreed to, and usually point to two or three they would not sign today.

In business this becomes a clock rule. Nothing that arrives with a charge on it gets a reply in the same hour: the hostile email, the complaint, the supplier's refusal. Draft the answer, leave it, come back after a meal. Within a month you will notice that on the second pass you are not changing the facts. You are deleting the sentences that existed to defend your pride, and those are the ones that cost money.
ch.cap: A student holds up his hand: wait, impression

ch.h: The iron lamp, the jug and the two handles
b: Epictetus taught in physical images, and three of them are worth carrying in your pocket. The first is a lamp. He kept an iron lamp beside the little shrine in his house. One night he heard a noise, went down, and found it stolen. His reaction, as he told his students, was not indifference. He admitted he had been beaten: the thief had got a lamp and paid for it with his honesty, a terrible bargain, while Epictetus had merely lost a lamp. Then the practical coda. Next time he bought an earthenware one. A man can only lose what he has.

The second is a jug. If you are fond of a jug, he says, tell yourself it is a jug you are fond of, a thing of fired clay, which breaks. Then when it breaks you will not be disturbed. He applies this, with a coldness that shocks modern readers, to the people we love: when you kiss your child, remind yourself that you are kissing a mortal. Whether that is wisdom or damage is a fair question, and Montaigne would answer it fifteen centuries later. But the structural point holds. Most grief is made worse by astonishment, and astonishment is the optional part.

The third is a handle. Everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it cannot. If your brother wrongs you, do not pick the matter up by the handle of he has wronged me, because that handle will not lift. Pick it up by the other: he is my brother, we were brought up together. Both descriptions are true. Only one can be acted on. Choosing it is not denial. It is selection.
ch.cap: A thief runs off with Epictetus's iron lamp

ch.h: The baths, the ship and the play
b: When you set out for the public baths, Epictetus says, picture what happens there: people splashing, people shoving, people being rude, people stealing. Then go, telling yourself that you want to bathe and also to keep your own will in harmony with nature. If someone splashes you, you expected it. Nobody has improved on this as advice for airports, customer service or Monday mornings.

On a sea voyage, he says, when the ship puts in for water, you may go ashore and pick up a shellfish or a little bulb along the way. But keep your mind on the ship and listen for the captain. If he calls, drop everything and run, or you will be thrown aboard tied up like the sheep. The shellfish are everything we gather in life. The captain's call is death. It is not a gloomy image. It is about carrying things lightly, and it plainly allows you to pick up the shellfish.

His picture of a whole life is the theatre. You are an actor in a play whose part was chosen by someone else. If it is a short part, play it well. If it is a beggar, a cripple, a ruler or a private citizen, play that. Your job is to perform the role, not to choose it.

This is often heard as passive: know your place. The life story alone refutes that. A slave who became a teacher of Rome's governing class did not think stations were fixed. His claim is narrower. At any given moment the externals are given: your age, your body, your market, this recession. What is not given is the quality of the performance, and the energy spent protesting the casting is simply taken away from the acting.
ch.cap: Passengers gather shellfish while the captain calls them back

ch.h: Sheep do not vomit up the grass
b: Epictetus had no patience with philosophy as a party trick. Never call yourself a philosopher, he tells his students, and do not talk much among ordinary people about your principles. Act on them. At a dinner, do not lecture people on how one ought to eat. Eat as one ought.

His image for this comes from the farmyard. Sheep do not bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they have eaten. They digest it inside and produce wool and milk outside. In the same way, a wrestler who has trained does not announce it. You look at his shoulders. The test of whether any of this has done you good is not that you can name the three disciplines. It is whether someone who does not know you have been reading notices, months later, that you are harder to rattle.

He also gives the hardest line in Stoicism its clearest form. Do not ask for things to happen as you wish, but wish them to happen as they do happen, and your life will go well. This is where many readers get off, and they are not being stupid. Taken literally it seems to forbid wanting the world to improve. The Stoic answer is that the wishing comes after the fact. You act hard to change what you can, and once the outcome is fixed you decline to spend the rest of your life arguing with it.

Epictetus died at Nicopolis, probably around 135 AD, an old man, poor and much loved. He never wrote a book. His student's notes would travel further than anything written by the emperors who had banished his kind.
ch.cap: Sheep quietly turn their grass into wool and milk

b: On 9 September 1965 a United States Navy commander called James Stockdale was flying an A-4 Skyhawk from the carrier Oriskany when it was hit by anti-aircraft fire over North Vietnam. Years earlier, as a graduate student at Stanford, he had been given a copy of the Enchiridion by a philosophy professor, and a fighter pilot carrying a Greek handbook was, he admitted, a slightly comic figure. As he ejected, by his own later account, he told himself that he was leaving the world of technology and entering the world of Epictetus.

He was right. His leg was badly broken on landing and he was beaten by the people who caught him. He was held for about seven and a half years, much of it in the prison Americans called the Hanoi Hilton, four years of it in solitary confinement, and he was tortured repeatedly. He was released in February 1973 and later received the Medal of Honor.

He wrote about it afterwards in openly Stoic terms. His captors controlled his body completely and his judgements not at all, and the distinction that had sounded like a classroom nicety in California turned out to be the only thing in the cell that was actually his.

Two cautions, so this is not a recruitment drive. First, the split between what is up to you and what is not is cleaner in logic than in life. Most things that matter, your health, your reputation, your business, respond to effort without being decided by it. The modern philosopher William Irvine suggests a third category, things partly up to you, where your goal is your own best effort rather than the outcome. Purists object, but it is the version a working person needs. Second, that is not up to you is a true sentence that can be turned into a weapon, used to tell people to stop complaining about things someone powerful is doing to them. Epictetus was talking about your inner state in conditions you cannot change. He had been owned. He knew the difference.
ch.cap: Stockdale parachutes into the world of Epictetus

take: Not your health, reputation, property or even your children: only the faculty that judges and chooses. Treating a loan as a possession is where the suffering starts.
Audit your worry in two columns
Write what is truly up to you against what is not, then check where last month's attention went. The fixable problem is usually sitting untouched in the left-hand column.
Impressions arrive already interpreted. Say, in effect, wait, let me test you, and the gap between event and agreement widens with practice.
Turn the gap into a clock rule
Nothing with a charge on it gets a same-hour reply. On the second pass you will be deleting the sentences that defended your pride, which are the expensive ones.
After the theft, Epictetus bought an earthenware lamp. When something is taken from you, neither rage nor simply forgive: work out what you are exposed to and adjust it.
Every situation has several true descriptions, and only some can be acted on. Choosing the one you can carry is selection, not denial.
Do not vomit up the grass
Never announce your principles; show them in your conduct. The test is whether people notice you are harder to rattle, not whether you can quote Stoics.
Use the trichotomy, and never as a weapon

Most important things are partly up to you, so aim at your own best effort and let the outcome be the outcome. Never use that is not in your control to silence someone being wronged by a person with power.
recall: State the dichotomy of control and name the one thing Epictetus says we truly own.

Up to us are judgement, impulse, desire and aversion, everything of our own doing; not up to us are body, property, reputation and position. The only thing we own is prohairesis, the reasoned will or faculty of choice.
What is the discipline of assent, and what should you say to an arriving impression?
It is the practice of withholding agreement from first impressions, which arrive already interpreted. You challenge it: wait for me a little, impression, let me see what you are and let me test you.
Explain the two handles and why choosing one is not self-deception.

Every event offers more than one true description, some of which can be carried and some not. He has wronged me and he is my brother are both true, but only the second can be acted on, so you are selecting between accurate descriptions rather than inventing a false one.
How do we know what Epictetus taught?

He wrote nothing. His student Arrian, later a consul and historian of Alexander, recorded his lectures in eight books of Discourses, four of which survive, and compiled the short Enchiridion or handbook. Arrian's life of Epictetus is lost.
What is William Irvine's trichotomy of control, and why does it matter?

It adds a third category, things partly up to us, where the right goal is your own best effort rather than the outcome. It matters because health, reputation and businesses respond to effort without being decided by it, which the strict two-way split does not describe.
note: Epictetus's life is thinly documented: his birthplace, slavery under Epaphroditus, study with Musonius Rufus, expulsion under Domitian and school at Nicopolis are reasonably secure, while his dates are approximate. The leg-breaking story comes only through Celsus as quoted by Origen and is probably apocryphal; the adopted child is reported by the later writer Simplicius, and the Hadrian friendship by the unreliable Historia Augusta. Stockdale's capture, imprisonment and Stoic account are in his own writings. The trichotomy is from William Irvine's A Guide to the Good Life, 2009.
words: The formal act of freeing a slave.

A showy display intended to impress others.
His image of sheep that do not vomit up their grass to show the shepherd is an attack on philosophical ostentation: digest it and let the wool show.
The belief that events are fixed and human effort cannot change them.
His picture of life as a role in a play is often misread as fatalism, but his own rise from slave to teacher shows he meant only that the given part is fixed at any moment, not the performance.

biz: Run the two-column audit on the brokerage

Take last month's worries and sort them. Not up to you: lender criteria, base rate, Google's algorithm, a lender's underwriting speed, a competitor's ad budget. Up to you: how fast an enquiry gets a first call, how many contact attempts you make and how polite they are, whether the landing page explains fees and that a secured loan risks the home, how well cases are packaged before they reach a lender. Most owners find the worry on the right and the fixable problem on the left. This week, measure speed to first contact and the share of enquiries reaching a full fact-find, and put your effort there.
Help distressed clients find their handle

Debt clients often arrive with everything on the right-hand column: bailiff letters, a partner's anger, a bank's tone. Train advisers to help them, gently, find the one or two things they can act on today, such as which priority bill to address first and what information to gather. Use Epictetus's two handles: the same situation can be picked up as I have failed or as here is the next step. Never turn it round into it is not up to you as a way to dismiss a complaint or a fear; Epictetus meant inner state, not excusing harm. Track how many first calls end with a clear agreed next action.
connects: Frankl's discovery in the camps that the last human freedom is to choose one's attitude is Epictetus's split between what is up to us and what is not, proved again in the twentieth century.
Epictetus's instruction to say wait for me a little, impression, is a deliberate pause that lets slow, reflective thinking check the fast intuitive verdict Kahneman describes.
Voss's hostage negotiator staying calm under threat and reframing the other side's position draws on the same move as Epictetus's two handles: choosing the description you can act on.
recap:
He was born a slave, around the middle of the first century, in a spa town in what is now Turkey. We do not even know his real name. The one history kept, Epictetus, simply means acquired. It is a label for property. As a boy he was taken to Rome, where his owner was Epaphroditus, one of Nero's secretaries, a man who lived at the dangerous centre of power. Epictetus walked with a limp, and nobody knows for certain why.

His owner did one thing that changed the history of philosophy. He let his slave attend the lectures of Musonius Rufus, the most serious Stoic teacher in Rome. Later Epictetus was freed and began to teach himself, until the Emperor Domitian threw the philosophers out of Rome. Epictetus crossed to Nicopolis on the Greek coast, opened a school for young men heading into government, and lived there on almost nothing for the rest of his life. He never wrote a word. A student called Arrian took notes, and those notes eventually reached Marcus Aurelius.

His central idea is a single division. Some things are up to us: our judgements, our desires, our choices. Everything else is not: our body, our property, our reputation, even the people we love. Treat only the first as truly yours, and nobody can compel you. That was not a metaphor for a man whose body had belonged to someone else.

From it comes his most quoted line. We are disturbed not by things, but by our judgements about things. An impression arrives already dressed up. You cannot stop it arriving, but you can decline to sign it. Wait for me a little, impression, he told his students. Let me test you.

He taught in pictures. A stolen iron lamp, replaced with a cheap clay one. A jug that you remind yourself can break. Everything has two handles, one you can carry it by and one you cannot. And life is a play: you did not choose the part, but you choose the performance.

Centuries later, an American pilot named James Stockdale ejected over North Vietnam and told himself he was entering the world of Epictetus. Through years of prison and torture, the division held.

Two cautions. Much of life is only partly up to us. And not up to you must never become a weapon to silence people who are being wronged.

The line to remember: you cannot stop the impression arriving, but you never have to sign it.
